stops.title: Before neurons

diverged_mya.node: Crown animals; context for both exemplars
diverged_mya.value_basis: Midpoint of the published composite interval, table 1; millions of years.

neuron_counts.method: Anatomical examination of contracting sponge tissue.
neuron_counts.evidence_quote: absence of neurons and true muscle

neuron_counts.method: Comparative cell descriptions and gene-activity surveys.

stops.summary: A freshwater sponge can flush waste by squeezing its canals. Trichoplax glides over algae, stops and releases digestive chemicals exactly where its meal lies. Both coordinate behavior without neurons.

structures.name: Digestive-chamber signaling
structures.description: In a freshwater sponge, cells with tiny secretory packets reach around neighboring feeding cells. Both use proteins also found at nerve junctions.
structures.species_context: Spongilla lacustris in the digestive-chamber experiment. Ephydatia muelleri in the canal-flushing experiment.

structures.name: Contractile sheets
structures.description: Sheets of sponge cells contain linked bundles of contractile fibers. Waves of tightening travel across them.
structures.evidence_quote: continuous tracts spanning the whole sponge
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

structures.name: Gliding hairs
structures.description: Tiny beating hairs carry Trichoplax across its food.

structures.name: Digestive secretory cells
structures.description: Individual Trichoplax cells release material that breaks open nearby algae.
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

abilities.name: Flush clogged canals
abilities.description: After mechanical stimulation, researchers watched waves of contraction push waste out of a freshwater sponge.

abilities.name: Park over food
abilities.description: Live imaging showed Trichoplax stopping its beating hairs over algae and gliding away after feeding.

abilities.name: Digest food on the spot
abilities.description: Live imaging caught only the cells beside algae releasing digestive packets.

inherited.name: Beating hairs used for movement long before animals diverged
inherited.evidence_quote: the last common ancestor of all eukaryotic organisms possessed a 9+2 flagellum

nuances.claim: A synapse gene means an animal has synapses.
nuances.reality: A marine sponge carries many genes for proteins used on the receiving side of a nerve junction. Anatomists have found no recognizable neuronal synapses.
nuances.evidence_quote: sponges lack neurons with clearly recognizable synapses

nuances.claim: Coordinated behavior requires neurons.
nuances.reality: Trichoplax stops, feeds and moves on without neurons. Researchers found multiple kinds of cells that send short chemical messages in placozoans.
nuances.evidence_quote: no neurons but also show coordinated behaviors triggered by peptide-secreting cells

nuances.claim: Which living lineage branches first in the animal tree?
nuances.reality: Schultz and colleagues found chromosome arrangements favoring comb jellies. Pisani and colleagues argued that some sequence analyses favor comb jellies because of how they model evolution. The position of the root and the origin of neurons are separate questions.
nuances.evidence_quote: placing ctenophores as the sister group to all other animals

connectome.description: These exemplars have no recognized neuronal synapses to map. Electron microscopy has mapped contacts among other kinds of cells.
connectome.evidence_quote: lack neurons with clearly recognizable synapses

open_question.text: What tells a whole Trichoplax to stop while only the cells beside food release digestive packets?

stops.title: Nerve nets

diverged_mya.node: Crown cnidarians (Hydra and box jelly); excludes comb jellies
diverged_mya.value_basis: Midpoint of the published composite interval, table 1; millions of years.

neuron_counts.region: cells in the illustrated whole-animal activity recording; one polyp
neuron_counts.method: Fluorescent activity imaging in a polyp with labeled neurons; identified cells in this recording.

neuron_counts.region: under-surface nerve net in the reconstructed larval volume only
neuron_counts.method: Three-dimensional electron microscopy; count of cell bodies in the sampled net.

neuron_counts.evidence_quote: rhopalial nervous system of approximately 1000 neurons

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: histochemical staining techniques and electron microscopy

stops.summary: A Hydra stretches and contracts with different networks. A box jellyfish can learn near its eyes. In a comb jelly, parts of a nerve net even share one continuous membrane. These are three different solutions to coordinating a body.

structures.name: Eye-bearing sensory centers
structures.description: The box jellyfish has four sensory centers connected to a nerve running around its bell. Each center brings eyes and nearby nerve tissue together.
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

structures.name: Body-wide activity networks
structures.description: In Hydra, distinct groups of neurons become active during different body movements.

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: as in many cnidarian polyps, are organized in a nerve net

structures.name: Continuous nerve net
structures.description: In the comb jelly studied, parts of the net just under the body surface share a continuous outer membrane.
structures.evidence_quote: a continuous plasma membrane that forms a syncytium
structures.origin_scope: Unknown for the continuous net. Independent and shared origins of neurons are both proposed; see the debate below.

abilities.name: Learn to avoid obstacles
abilities.description: In a tank experiment, Caribbean box jellyfish learned to combine visual contrast with contact. Tests on isolated sensory centers linked learning to those centers.
abilities.evidence_quote: combines visual and mechanical stimuli during operant conditioning

abilities.name: Shorten the body
abilities.description: Researchers filmed activity throughout Hydra and saw one network light up during lengthwise contractions.

abilities.name: Lengthen in response to light
abilities.description: A different network lit up as Hydra lengthened in response to light.

inherited.name: An older toolkit for sending and receiving chemical signals

nuances.claim: Did neurons arise independently in comb jellies?
nuances.reality: Moroz and colleagues interpret unusual signaling chemistry as evidence for independent origins. Jékely and colleagues point to shared signaling molecules and sensory cells consistent with common ancestry.
nuances.evidence_quote: ctenophore neural systems, and possibly muscle specification, evolved independently

nuances.claim: A box jellyfish spreads all processing evenly through its net.
nuances.reality: Its ring nerve runs into four eye-bearing centers. The obstacle-learning experiment localized learning to these sensory centers.
nuances.evidence_quote: one coherent CNS including the rhopalia

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: rhopalial nervous system is the learning center

connectome.description: Volume electron microscopy traced a young comb jelly’s under-surface net. A separate Hydra study imaged bundles of nerve fibers. Neither project claims every connection in the animal.
connectome.evidence_quote: three-dimensional reconstructions to characterize the nerve net

open_question.text: Which features of comb-jelly neurons can distinguish a shared origin from independent invention?
open_question.evidence_quote: consistent with a shared ancestry of nervous systems

stops.title: Heads

diverged_mya.node: Crown bilaterians; shared ancestral context for the trail
diverged_mya.value_basis: Midpoint of the published composite interval, table 1; millions of years.

neuron_counts.method: Reconstruction from electron micrographs of consecutive tissue slices.

neuron_counts.region: neuronal nodes in the published adult male reference graph
neuron_counts.method: Cook and colleagues combined serial electron microscopy reconstructions; this number describes the published graph.

stops.summary: A flatworm can weigh the pull of a chemical against the glare of light. A roundworm switches from tight turns to wider exploration after it loses food. Both examples let researchers connect choices to particular neurons.

structures.name: Planarian brain
structures.description: In the flatworm’s head, a brain receives several kinds of sensory input. Which input wins can depend on light intensity.
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: counting the numbers of specific neurons in the eye and brain

structures.name: Longitudinal nerve bundles
structures.description: In the roundworm, bundles of nerve fibers run lengthwise. Neighbors make many of their connections locally.
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

structures.name: Search circuit
structures.description: Smell and taste cells feed roundworm neurons that change the frequency of turns and reversals.
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

abilities.name: Choose between food cues and light
abilities.description: Given an attractive chemical and light together, planarians followed the chemical under dimmer conditions and increasingly avoided stronger light.

abilities.name: Follow chemical cues
abilities.description: Suppressing nerve transmission in the regenerated head disrupted the flatworm’s movement toward chemicals.
abilities.evidence_quote: lost both chemotactic and thigmotactic behaviors

abilities.name: Search near a lost meal
abilities.description: After removal from food, roundworms backed up and made tight turns. Manipulating identified neurons separated local searching from later dispersal.

inherited.name: Neurons and their shared developmental machinery
inherited.evidence_quote: last common ancestor of Bilateria and Cnidaria was an animal with a well-established nervous system

nuances.claim: Every adult C. elegans has exactly the same nervous system.
nuances.reality: The familiar count describes the adult hermaphrodite. Whole-animal maps show differences between adult sexes, including in connections between neurons they share.
nuances.evidence_quote: differs between sexes

nuances.claim: The original wiring map captured every junction.
nuances.reality: White and colleagues described most identifiable connections. Later work combined new and older images to extend the maps to both sexes.
nuances.evidence_quote: Most of the morphologically identifiable

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: for the first time the complete set of synaptic connections

nuances.claim: Did the common ancestor of bilaterians already have a brain?
nuances.reality: Northcutt argues for independent centralization from a diffuse net. Holland and colleagues argue that shared developmental patterns favor an ancestral central nervous system.
nuances.evidence_quote: brains evolved independently at least four times

connectome.description: Whole-animal reference maps for both adult sexes combine reconstructions across specimens and image series. Completeness describes anatomical scope.
connectome.evidence_quote: new and previously published electron micrographs

open_question.text: Which differences in connection strength between the sexes actually change behavior?

stops.title: Arthropod brains

diverged_mya.node: Arthropod and nematode lineages in the sampled tree
diverged_mya.value_basis: Midpoint of the published composite interval, table 1; millions of years.

neuron_counts.region: adult female brain, including visual lobes
neuron_counts.method: FlyWire reconstruction from serial electron microscopy.

neuron_counts.region: class I Kenyon cells per mushroom body; approximate
neuron_counts.estimate_text: The review reports a regional anatomical estimate and distinguishes two cell classes. The original counting protocol was not verified.

stops.summary: A walking fly keeps track of which way it faces even when the lights go out. In a honeybee, the activity leaving a learning center changes when a familiar smell predicts food.

structures.name: Heading compass
structures.description: A ring-shaped part of the fly’s central complex carries a moving pattern of activity that tracks the direction the fly faces.
structures.origin_scope: The inherited structure is the insect central complex. The fly experiment identifies a heading signal in one part of it.

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: sky compass orientation, and integration of spatial information

structures.name: Mushroom bodies
structures.description: These insect brain centers combine sensory information. In honeybees their output changes after an odor predicts a reward.
structures.evidence_quote: Mushroom body output neurons encode odor-reward associations

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: olfactory input to the mushroom body calyces in more recent insect orders is an acquired character

structures.origin_scope: Elaboration of smell input to the mushroom bodies; the date of the first mushroom body is a separate question.

structures.name: Visual lobes
structures.description: These paired fly brain regions connect with the central brain. Electron microscopy lets researchers trace paths from light sensors toward movement circuits.
structures.evidence_quote: central brain and the optic lobes
structures.origin_scope: Comparison of visual lobes in insects and crustaceans; applies to the shared processing regions.

abilities.name: Keep a heading in the dark
abilities.description: As flies walked on a ball, the heading signal kept updating from the flies’ own movements after the lights went out.

abilities.name: Orient to landmarks
abilities.description: Imaging walking flies in virtual reality showed that the same activity pattern tracked visible landmarks.

abilities.name: Remember a rewarded odor
abilities.description: Bees learned to extend their feeding tube for an odor. Hours later, activity leaving the mushroom bodies distinguished the rewarded smell.
abilities.evidence_quote: associative plastic changes occurred only during retention 3 h after conditioning

inherited.name: Neurons connected into sensory and movement circuits

nuances.claim: The fly number counts every neuron in its body.
nuances.reality: The count is for one adult female fruit fly brain. It includes the visual lobes.
nuances.evidence_quote: 139,255 neurons

nuances.claim: A compass needs a landmark at every moment.
nuances.reality: The heading signal can persist even when the fly stops receiving both visual and movement cues.
nuances.evidence_quote: persistent activity

connectome.description: FlyWire mapped chemical connections across one adult female fly brain. In honeybees, a separate study reconstructed small clusters of input synapses in the mushroom bodies.
connectome.project_scope: complete refers to the adult female fly brain; honeybee coverage is partial.

open_question.text: Which of the routes from photoreceptors to movement neurons actually control a given visual behavior?

stops.title: Cephalopods

diverged_mya.node: Crown cephalopods; nautilus and coleoid lineages
diverged_mya.value_basis: Published clock estimate and 95% credible interval.

neuron_counts.method: Historical regional anatomical estimates summed across lobes and ganglia.
Historical estimates for clusters of nerve cells in the arms.

stops.summary: A common octopus carries most of its neurons in its arms. An arm can produce part of a reach locally, while a learning center in the head helps the animal remember which objects to avoid.

structures.name: Arm nerve cords
structures.description: An octopus arm contains circuitry that can produce a coordinated reach locally.
structures.evidence_quote: neural circuitry of the arm itself
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

structures.name: Contact-taste receptors
structures.description: Specialized proteins in octopus suckers detect substances that dissolve poorly in seawater. Contact makes these substances available to the animal.
structures.evidence_quote: a family of cephalopod-specific chemotactile receptors

structures.name: Vertical lobe
structures.description: The vertical lobe supports memory. Its wiring resembles circuits used in other animals for learning associations. The claim of convergence concerns the arrangement of connections.
structures.evidence_quote: the VL has evolved a unique circuit

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: independently evolved twice on this planet
sharing morphological and wiring features with circuits supporting associative learning in other animals

abilities.name: Extend an arm
abilities.description: Mechanical or electrical stimulation produced a reach-like extension even after researchers disconnected an arm from the brain.
abilities.evidence_quote: connection with the brain has been severed

abilities.name: Taste a surface
abilities.description: Receptor tests and recordings from sensory cells showed how the California two-spot octopus detects prey chemicals by touch.

abilities.name: Acquire lasting memories
abilities.description: After researchers cut or electrically stimulated a vertical-lobe pathway, octopuses were worse the next day at remembering an object they had learned to avoid.
abilities.evidence_quote: both treatments impaired long-term recall the next day

inherited.name: A nervous system inherited from the common ancestor of bilaterians and cnidarians

nuances.claim: Each arm is an independent animal.
nuances.reality: The arm can generate part of a reach locally. Normal movement also engages circuits in the central brain.
nuances.evidence_quote: engages every division of the octopus nervous system

nuances.claim: Most of the octopus’s neurons sit between its eyes.
nuances.reality: Young estimated about 300 million arm neurons out of about 500 million neurons in a common octopus.
nuances.evidence_quote: 500 million nerve cells

connectome.description: Serial electron microscopy mapped a small piece of the common octopus’s vertical lobe, including two interconnected learning pathways.

open_question.text: How does the central brain recruit local arm programs during an ordinary reach?
open_question.evidence_quote: open questions and areas for further study

stops.title: Chordate origins

diverged_mya.node: Crown chordates; lancelet lineage versus tunicates and vertebrates
diverged_mya.value_basis: Midpoint of the published composite interval, table 1; millions of years.

neuron_counts.region: larval central nervous system; species name as published
neuron_counts.method: Electron microscopy of consecutive tissue slices.

stops.summary: A swimming sea squirt larva has separate routes for light direction and sudden dimming. When the animal changes shape, some larval cells help rebuild its adult nervous system. A lancelet’s frontal eye offers another clue to the shared history of chordate senses.

structures.name: Dorsal nerve tube
structures.description: The sea squirt larva has a hollow central nervous system running along its back. This overall layout is shared across chordates.

structures.name: Two visual routes
structures.description: In sea squirt larvae, different light-sensitive cells feed separate routes to swimming muscles. One responds to light direction, the other to dimming.
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

structures.name: Frontal eye
structures.description: Light-sensitive and pigment cells in the lancelet’s front eye share molecular features with cells in the vertebrate retina, the eye’s light-sensitive tissue.
structures.evidence_quote: homology between amphioxus frontal eye and vertebrate eyes
structures.origin_scope: Applies to the underlying anatomical structure; the date of the measured response is unknown.

structures.name: Nerve-tube lining cells
structures.description: Some cells lining the larval sea squirt nervous system can generate adult neurons as the animal changes shape.
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

abilities.name: Swim in response to light direction
abilities.description: Combining a wiring map with behavioral tests identified a route from light-sensitive cells toward motor neurons that responds to directional light.

abilities.name: Escape when light fades
abilities.description: Blocking a chemical signal and testing larvae with missing light sensors helped identify a separate escape route triggered by dimming.

abilities.name: Rebuild the adult nervous system
abilities.description: By labeling and following individual cells through the larva’s transformation, researchers found that some lining cells became adult neurons.

inherited.name: Genes that pattern the body and nervous system from head to tail
inherited.evidence_quote: similarly expressed both in the CNS and in the remainder of the ectoderm in many bilaterians

nuances.claim: The sea squirt eats its whole brain.
nuances.reality: Many larval neurons disappear, but tracing marked cells showed that some neurons persist and other larval cells help build the adult nervous system.
nuances.evidence_quote: a subset of cholinergic motor neurons

nuances.claim: Matching numbers on both sides mean matching wiring.
nuances.reality: The sea squirt larva has equal numbers of cells on its two sides, yet the identities and pathways can differ.
nuances.evidence_quote: pathways differ left/right

connectome.description: Serial electron microscopy mapped the central nervous system of a swimming Ciona intestinalis larva. The Pacific Ciona robusta used in behavioral studies is a separate species.

open_question.text: Which lancelet and vertebrate eye cells descend from the same ancestral cell types?

stops.title: First vertebrates

diverged_mya.node: Crown vertebrates; jawless versus jawed vertebrate lineages
diverged_mya.value_basis: Midpoint of the published composite interval, table 1; millions of years.

neuron_counts.region: whole brain; modeled estimate from four river lampreys
neuron_counts.method: Counted nuclei in dispersed tissue, then estimated the neuronal share using a ratio extrapolated from other species.
neuron_counts.evidence_quote: the total neuron number ntotal was approximated

stops.summary: A lamprey can turn toward a slowly moving object or away from a looming one. Its brain shares movement-control circuits with mammals, including routes that restrain other movement centers.

structures.name: Basal ganglia
structures.description: These connected forebrain centers regulate pathways for movement. Lampreys and mammals share both the main centers and the direct and indirect routes between them.
structures.origin_scope: Vertebrate circuit shared by lampreys and mammals. Its deeper origin remains open.

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: suggests deep homology of arthropod central complex and vertebrate basal ganglia

structures.name: Visual orienting center
structures.description: The optic tectum links sight to movement. In a lamprey, its output can recruit different circuits depending on how an object moves.
structures.origin_scope: Shared across vertebrates.

structures.name: Descending movement pathways
structures.description: Nerve cells in the brainstem send commands toward the spinal cord. The visual orienting center uses these routes to steer responses.

abilities.name: Gate candidate movements
abilities.description: Tracing and electrical recordings showed that lamprey output cells continually restrain movement centers. Researchers infer a role in selecting actions.
abilities.evidence_quote: pallidal output neurons tonically inhibit tectum

abilities.name: Turn toward a moving object
abilities.description: In an eye–brain–spinal cord preparation, slowly moving targets triggered one-sided nerve activity corresponding to a turn.

abilities.name: Switch to avoidance
abilities.description: Rapidly looming targets triggered an avoidance pattern. Blocking particular signals in the visual center changed which motor pattern appeared.

inherited.name: Regional organization of the developing nerve tube
inherited.evidence_quote: amphioxus shares multiple features of this bauplan

nuances.claim: All vertebrates wrap their nerve fibers in myelin.
nuances.reality: Lampreys and hagfish lack the tightly layered insulating wrap called myelin. Neighboring support cells can still surround nerve fibers.
nuances.evidence_quote: both lamprey and hagfish lack myelin

nuances.claim: Did the lamprey inherit a cerebellum?
nuances.reality: Sugahara and colleagues found developmental signals resembling those that build a cerebellum. Lamanna and colleagues found no convincing counterparts of its characteristic mature cell types. These are different tests of ancestry.
nuances.evidence_quote: ancestral genetic programs for the formation of a distinct cerebellum

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: did not provide evidence for the presence of granule or Purkinje cells

connectome.description: In river lamprey retina, researchers labeled nerve fibers arriving from the brain and identified their local synaptic targets by electron microscopy.
connectome.evidence_quote: the centrifugal terminals synapse either upon unlabeled somata or profiles containing synaptic vesicles

open_question.text: How much of the ancestral cerebellum can be identified from developmental signals when mature cell types give a different answer?
open_question.evidence_quote: probably devoid of cerebellar cell types

stops.title: Jawed fish

diverged_mya.node: Crown jawed vertebrates; cartilaginous versus bony vertebrates
diverged_mya.value_basis: Midpoint of the published composite interval, table 1; millions of years.

neuron_counts.region: olfactory bulb of one larval zebrafish; reconstructed neurons
neuron_counts.method: Three-dimensional electron microscopy and cell tracing.
neuron_counts.estimate_text: Over 1,000 neurons were reconstructed in one larval zebrafish smell center.

neuron_counts.region: ganglion cells in one retina across adult goldfish of different sizes
neuron_counts.method: Counts of cell nuclei in tissue sections, scaled by measured retinal area.
neuron_counts.estimate_text: About 60,000 to 350,000 output neurons per adult goldfish retina across the sampled sizes.

neuron_counts.region: whole larval brain; order of magnitude only
neuron_counts.method: Review estimate based on stereological sampling: count cells in tissue samples and scale to brain volume.
neuron_counts.evidence_quote: total number of neurons is on the order of
neuron_counts.estimate_text: On the order of 10⁵ neurons in a larval zebrafish brain. The value encodes the order of magnitude.

stops.summary: A goldfish can remember a place, a shark can steer by which nostril smells an odor first, and an electric fish can learn while sensing. Experiments let us name different circuits and signals behind each ability.

structures.name: Myelin
structures.description: In jawed vertebrates, support cells wrap nerve fibers in compact layers of insulation. This entry dates the vertebrate version of the wrap.
structures.evidence_quote: in ancestors of the living cartilaginous fishes

structures.name: Layered cerebellum
structures.description: Two signature types of cerebellar neuron develop in distinct places. The shared layout is recognizable across living jawed vertebrates.
structures.evidence_quote: shared in all extant jawed vertebrates

structures.name: Spatial-memory forebrain
structures.description: The lateral pallium, part of the goldfish forebrain, supports memory for places. Damage there affects navigation much as damage to the mammalian hippocampus does.
structures.origin_scope: The broad forebrain territory is inherited. Lesions test function; matching individual subdivisions across fish and mammals also requires anatomical and developmental evidence.

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: homologues of the olfactory pallium, hippocampus, and pallial amygdala

structures.name: Paired smell inputs
structures.description: A smooth dogfish can compare when odor reaches the two sides of its snout.
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

structures.name: Electric-sense lobe
structures.description: This processing center in an electric fish learns while it continues to transmit signals. Different parts of the same cells can carry different signals.
structures.evidence_quote: functional compartmentalization within intermediate layer neurons
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

abilities.name: Remember a place
abilities.description: Goldfish with damage to the lateral pallium struggled to find a remembered location. They could still follow a visible cue.

abilities.name: Follow an odor plume
abilities.description: Researchers delivered carefully timed pulses into each nostril. Smooth dogfish turned toward the side that got the odor first, even when the later pulse was stronger.
abilities.evidence_quote: They turned toward the side stimulated first

abilities.name: Learn while sensing
abilities.description: Recordings in electric fish showed how the same network carries sensory output while updating its response to repeated input.
abilities.evidence_quote: reconcile learning and signaling functions without switching its mode of operation

inherited.name: Basal ganglia circuits that regulate movement

nuances.claim: A fish has no counterpart to the mammalian memory forebrain.
nuances.reality: Goldfish and turtle lesion experiments support a shared spatial-memory system. They test one functional correspondence, leaving other region-by-region matches open.
nuances.evidence_quote: map-like memory representations

nuances.claim: Imaging an entire brain gives a complete wiring diagram.
nuances.reality: Researchers imaged an entire larval zebrafish brain and traced its myelinated fibers. The published reconstruction covers a subset of all circuits.
nuances.evidence_quote: survey all myelinated axons

nuances.claim: Only vertebrates invented nerve insulation.
nuances.reality: Some segmented worms and crustaceans also wrap nerve fibers in layers. Comparative anatomy supports separate origins of these wraps.
nuances.evidence_quote: arisen independently in evolution several times

connectome.description: In a larval zebrafish smell center, researchers reconstructed nearly all neurons and marked synapses on selected cells. A separate project imaged the whole larval brain and traced selected pathways.
connectome.evidence_quote: annotated all synapses on subsets of neurons
connectome.project_scope: partial refers to traced connectivity, including the larval smell center.

open_question.text: Which connections explain the activity of each identified nerve fiber in a behaving zebrafish?
open_question.evidence_quote: set the stage for whole-brain structure-function comparisons

stops.title: Onto land

diverged_mya.node: Crown tetrapods; amphibian versus amniote lineages
diverged_mya.value_basis: Midpoint of the published composite interval, table 1; millions of years.

neuron_counts.method: Anatomical and physiological literature synthesis; approximate scale only.
neuron_counts.estimate_text: A hatchling clawed frog has a few thousand neurons.

stops.summary: Between a touch and a tadpole’s first swim stroke, nerve cells build up activity. In some salamanders, evolution reduced the number and variety of visual neurons while the animals continued to rely on vision.

structures.name: Swimming command neurons
structures.description: In frog tadpoles, cells near the back of the brain receive touch-related signals. Swimming starts when enough excitation builds up.

structures.name: Visual orienting center
structures.description: In the Italian cave salamander, neurons in this midbrain area respond to moving shapes with different sizes and orientations.
structures.evidence_quote: responded selectively to moving visual stimuli
structures.origin_scope: Applies to the underlying anatomical structure; the date of the measured response is unknown.

structures.name: Large, sparsely packed visual neurons
structures.description: Some salamanders have relatively few, large neurons in the visual system. Comparisons among relatives suggest that this arrangement arose through secondary simplification.
structures.origin_scope: Applies to the underlying anatomical structure; the date of the measured response is unknown.

structures.name: Midbrain steering pathways
structures.description: Signals from the midbrain influence the timing and direction of swimming in a newly hatched clawed frog.

abilities.name: Start swimming after a touch
abilities.description: Electrical recordings in hatchling frog tadpoles showed nerve activity accumulating between a brief touch and the first swimming command.

abilities.name: Distinguish moving shapes
abilities.description: Recordings from Italian cave salamanders separated cells that responded differently to squares and to vertical or horizontal rectangles.
abilities.evidence_quote: differed strongly in their responses to rectangles

abilities.name: Steer after a touch
abilities.description: Tadpoles kept swimming after small midbrain injuries, but the time they took to start and the path they swam changed.

inherited.name: Descending control of spinal swimming circuits

nuances.claim: Similar-looking brain regions always preserve the ancestral arrangement.
nuances.reality: Comparisons across salamanders suggest some lineages secondarily reduced the number and variety of visual neurons. The proposed role of genome size is a further hypothesis.
nuances.evidence_quote: derived secondarily from a more complex ancestral state

nuances.claim: A touch triggers an immediate fixed swimming reflex.
nuances.reality: The delay varies in hatchling frogs. A brief touch can leave a longer-lasting trace in the swimming circuit.
nuances.evidence_quote: memory of the sensory stimulus

connectome.description: Time-lapse imaging and electron microscopy identified and reconstructed synapses on individual visual-center neurons in clawed frog tadpoles.
connectome.evidence_quote: electron microscope reconstructions of imaged neurons

open_question.text: Which upstream neurons maintain the brief memory of touch in a frog tadpole?

stops.title: Reptiles

diverged_mya.node: Crown amniotes; reptile and mammal lineages
diverged_mya.value_basis: Midpoint of the published composite interval, table 1; millions of years.

neuron_counts.region: whole brain; one female red-eared slider
neuron_counts.method: Tissue dispersed into nuclei, followed by counts of labeled neuronal nuclei; supplementary datasets 1 and 2.

stops.summary: A turtle remembers places using a part of its forebrain that shares features with our hippocampus. Gene activity in turtles and lizards also reveals forebrain cell families that reptiles and mammals inherited together.

structures.name: Medial cortex
structures.description: A part of the turtle forebrain helps remember places relative to their surroundings. Its anatomy and function link it with the mammalian hippocampus.
structures.origin_scope: Applies to the underlying anatomical structure; the date of the measured response is unknown.

structures.name: Local inhibitory neurons
structures.description: These cells reduce activity in nearby neurons. Comparing gene activity in lizards and turtles traced several classes back to the common ancestor of reptiles and mammals.

structures.name: Retinal dopamine cells
structures.description: In the turtle’s eye, a branching nerve cell receives input from several types of neighbor. Researchers paired recordings with microscope reconstructions.
structures.evidence_quote: Bipolar ribbon synapses occurred in all three dendritic tiers
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

abilities.name: Find a place from a new start
abilities.description: Intact turtles swam to a goal from new starting points. Damaging this region impaired that ability in a maze.

abilities.name: Change a learned route
abilities.description: After damage to this brain region, turtles could relearn a place task. Probe trials showed that they now solved it differently.

abilities.name: Register sustained light
abilities.description: Recordings from turtle retinal cells showed a response that could outlast a bright flash. Electron microscopy identified their local connections.

inherited.name: A forebrain system that supports memory for places

nuances.claim: A reptile brain survives as an instinct-only core inside the human brain.
nuances.reality: Cesario, Johnson and Eisthen review why the three-part model fails. Reptiles and mammals inherited forebrain circuits that changed along both branches.
nuances.evidence_quote: has long been discredited among neurobiologists

nuances.claim: A memory area has to look like a human hippocampus to do similar work.
nuances.reality: Damage to the turtle medial cortex selectively disrupted place-based navigation, while turtles could still use a single visual cue.
nuances.evidence_quote: single intramaze visual cue

connectome.description: Serial electron microscopy reconstructed local inputs and outputs of a dopamine-producing cell in turtle retina. This is a cell-centered map.
connectome.evidence_quote: EM reconstruction of a Toh-IR cell revealed new circuitry

open_question.text: Which reptile forebrain cells share an ancestor with particular mammalian cortical cells?

stops.title: Birds

diverged_mya.node: Crown Neoaves as inferred by Stiller and colleagues; this includes the crow and parrot lineages.
diverged_mya.value_basis: Published clock estimate and 95% credible interval; younger than the bird–crocodilian split.

neuron_counts.method: Nuclear counting with the isotropic fractionator; supplementary table S1, counts in millions.

neuron_counts.region: whole brain; average of three budgerigars
neuron_counts.method: Nuclear counting with the isotropic fractionator; supplementary table S1, counts in millions.

stops.summary: Large parrots and crows can fit as many forebrain neurons as some much larger primates into a smaller brain. In a crow doing a visual task, the timing of individual neurons can predict whether the bird will report seeing a target.

structures.name: Crow and parrot pallium
structures.description: Large parrots and members of the crow family pack enough neurons into the pallium, the outer forebrain, to match some much larger primate brains.
structures.origin_scope: Applies to the underlying anatomical structure; the date of the measured response is unknown.

structures.name: Parrot vocal core and shell
structures.description: Parrots have a vocal circuit with an outer shell surrounding a core. Comparisons with other vocal-learning birds identify the shell as a parrot specialization.
structures.evidence_quote: "shell" song system is unique to parrots
structures.origin_scope: New outer shell in parrots; applies to the shell specifically.

structures.name: Tool-related circuits
structures.description: In American crows skilled at a stone-tool task, several regions including the cerebellum became more active as the birds prepared to act.
structures.evidence_quote: increase activity in circuits associated with motor learning and tactile control
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

abilities.name: Report a faint visual stimulus
abilities.description: In trained carrion crows, early activity in this region tracked stimulus strength. Later activity predicted the bird’s report. The recordings did not test whether neuron density explains performance.
abilities.evidence_quote: later component predicts the crows' perceptual reports

abilities.name: Learn vocal sounds
abilities.description: Researchers compared gene activity during singing and traced connections. They identified linked circuits used in vocal learning, with a distinctive outer shell in parrots.

abilities.name: Prepare to use a stone tool
abilities.description: Brain imaging compared trained and inexperienced American crows. The regions recruited before a stone-tool task differed with proficiency.
abilities.evidence_quote: talent affects the neural circuits activated by crows

inherited.name: An inherited forebrain system for remembering places

nuances.claim: A small brain necessarily has few forebrain neurons.
nuances.reality: A blue-and-yellow macaw has about 1.9 billion neurons in its pallium. Regional counts, brain mass and neuron density answer different questions.
nuances.evidence_quote: primates with much larger brains

nuances.claim: A recording from a living crow can tell us when conscious sensation originated.
nuances.reality: Nieder and colleagues discuss both a shared origin and separate origins. Their experiment measures activity that predicts a report in a living bird. It cannot distinguish those evolutionary histories.
nuances.evidence_quote: either before the emergence of mammals or independently

connectome.description: A synaptic map for the listed crow or parrot species was not verified. A chicken comparison is available.

comparative_projects.name: Chicken outer-retina reconstruction
comparative_projects.evidence_quote: contacts to other photoreceptor and bipolar cells in the chicken retina

open_question.text: What does the parrot’s outer vocal shell contribute to its ability to copy sounds?
open_question.evidence_quote: differences in vocal and cognitive abilities

stops.title: Early mammals

neuron_counts.region: whole brain; mean for four adult male Swiss mice
neuron_counts.method: Nuclear counting with the isotropic fractionator; table 1, counts in millions.

neuron_counts.region: neocortex of one hemisphere; group mean
neuron_counts.method: Dissected one cortical hemisphere and counted neuronal nuclei with the isotropic fractionator.

stops.summary: A mouse and an opossum both feel through their whiskers. Their touch maps differ, and their brain halves use different bridges to communicate. The six-layer cortical plan is older than the placental mammal’s corpus callosum.

structures.name: Six-layer neocortex
structures.description: The outer processing sheet of mammals has a distinctive six-layer plan. It developed from an older forebrain territory shared with reptiles.
structures.origin_scope: New six-layer arrangement of the inherited pallium.

structures.name: Anterior commissure
structures.description: This older bridge carries signals between brain halves. Marsupials and egg-laying mammals route connections between their cortical areas through it.

structures.name: Corpus callosum
structures.description: Placental mammals have a separate bridge between the brain halves. An opossum uses the older route for corresponding connections.
structures.origin_scope: New within placental mammals, after their divergence from marsupials.

structures.name: Whisker touch area
structures.description: In the opossum’s touch cortex, neurons can respond to several whiskers and usually respond most strongly to one.

abilities.name: Locate touch on the whiskers
abilities.description: Researchers moved individual opossum whiskers and recorded cortical neurons. Neighboring whiskers often activated the same cell to different degrees.

abilities.name: Exchange signals between hemispheres
abilities.description: Fiber imaging and cell tracing in a marsupial revealed organized routes connecting matching and different cortical areas on opposite sides.

abilities.name: Process visual patterns
abilities.description: In an awake mouse watching natural and synthetic images, researchers measured nerve activity and matched it to reconstructed visual cortex circuits.
abilities.evidence_quote: in an awake mouse that is viewing natural and synthetic stimuli

inherited.name: Forebrain inhibitory cells inherited from the common ancestor of reptiles and mammals

nuances.claim: Every mammal has a corpus callosum.
nuances.reality: Marsupials and egg-laying mammals connect their cortical hemispheres using the anterior commissure. Placental mammals evolved the extra bridge.
nuances.evidence_quote: separate commissural tract

nuances.claim: Whiskers require a barrel-shaped brain map.
nuances.reality: The opossum actively moves its whiskers and has touch-sensitive cortical neurons even though its cortex lacks the barrel-shaped clusters seen in mice.
nuances.evidence_quote: lack barrels and septa

connectome.description: MICrONS paired visual responses in a living mouse with electron microscopy of the same cortical tissue. The map includes several visual areas in one animal.
connectome.evidence_quote: electron microscopy reconstruction containing more than 200,000 cells and 0.5 billion synapses

open_question.text: Which aspects of mouse whisker processing also work in a cortex without barrels?

stops.title: Mammal radiations

neuron_counts.region: brain excluding olfactory bulbs; one adult African elephant, approximate
neuron_counts.method: Tissue divided by region, dispersed into nuclei and counted with neuronal labeling.
Region-by-region nuclear counting.

neuron_counts.region: auditory ganglion of the inner ear; anatomical estimate
neuron_counts.method: Anatomical count of nerve-cell bodies in the cochlea, the coiled hearing organ.

stops.summary: A flying bat’s hippocampus represents positions in three dimensions. A dolphin can group its clicks while approaching a distant target. In the African elephant examined, the cerebellum accounts for nearly all brain neurons.

structures.name: Three-dimensional place cells
structures.description: In flying bats, some memory-region neurons become active when the animal enters a particular volume of space.
structures.origin_scope: Applies to the underlying anatomical structure; the date of the measured response is unknown.

structures.name: Echo-ranging system
structures.description: Echolocating bats and toothed whales independently acquired echo-based sensing. In both groups, changes appeared in a protein used by sound-sensitive cells.
structures.evidence_quote: convergent amino acid substitutions in echolocating dolphins
structures.origin_scope: Convergence between echolocating bats and toothed whales. Place-cell recordings and hearing-gene comparisons sampled different animals.

structures.name: Neuron-rich cerebellum
structures.description: The African elephant brain examined had an especially large share of its neurons in the cerebellum. The reason for this concentration is still open.
structures.origin_scope: Elaboration of the inherited cerebellum in the elephant lineage; measured from one animal.

abilities.name: Represent a flight path in three dimensions
abilities.description: Wireless recordings in freely flying bats found different cells active in different volumes, together covering the available room.

abilities.name: Approach a distant target
abilities.description: Researchers put sound recording tags on trained bottlenose dolphins. Their click timing changed with target distance as they swam toward it.

abilities.name: Switch how clicks are grouped
abilities.description: At longer ranges, the dolphins frequently sent packets of clicks before waiting for returning echoes. Individual animals used different timing strategies.

nuances.claim: Three times as many neurons means three times as many cortical neurons.
nuances.reality: The sampled African elephant had about 257 billion brain neurons. About 251 billion were in its cerebellum and about 5.6 billion in its cerebral cortex.
nuances.evidence_quote: 5.6 billion neurons

nuances.claim: A dolphin must wait for each echo before making another click.
nuances.reality: Free-swimming bottlenose dolphins could group clicks into packets at long range.
nuances.evidence_quote: not a fixed echolocation strategy

connectome.description: No connectivity map was verified for the three listed species. A comparative study identified nerve endings on sensory cells in the ear of a mustached bat.

comparative_projects.name: Mustached bat cochlear terminal study
comparative_projects.evidence_quote: every OHC had a single, large terminal

open_question.text: Do the elephant’s unusually numerous cerebellar neurons support special demands on sensing and movement?

stops.title: Primates and humans
stops.clade: Primates: apes and Old World monkeys

diverged_mya.value_basis: Midpoint of approximate literature range in the introduction; not a confidence interval.

neuron_counts.region: whole brain; mean in the adult male sample
neuron_counts.method: Isotropic fractionator: disperse tissue, count nuclei, identify neurons with a marker.
Same nuclear count, rounded from the reported cortical share of the total.

neuron_counts.region: brain excluding olfactory bulbs; two young adults, group estimate
neuron_counts.method: Counted nuclei in one hemisphere and doubled the result. The later comparative paper identifies these animals as rhesus macaques.

stops.summary: The measured adult human brain averages about 86 billion neurons. Regional counts tell a different story from skull volume, the measure fossils preserve. Recordings in living people reveal that individual neurons can respond to different pictures of the same person.

structures.name: Action-responsive motor cortex
structures.description: Some macaque motor-planning neurons fire during both a mouth action and observation of a similar action by another individual.
structures.evidence_quote: execution and observation of mouth actions
structures.origin_scope: Elaboration of inherited mammalian cortex; the first appearance of matching action responses is undated.

structures.name: Identity-sensitive temporal neurons
structures.description: Some human neurons on the inner side of the temporal lobe respond to very different pictures of the same person or landmark.
structures.origin_scope: The observation is documented. The available evidence does not date the origin of this particular feature.

structures.name: Speech-sensitive parietal cortex
structures.description: Researchers recording individual neurons near the side of the human brain found signals related to words participants spoke silently.
structures.evidence_quote: significant neural representation of internal and vocalized speech
structures.origin_scope: Elaboration of inherited mammalian cortex; the experiment does not date silent speech.

abilities.name: Represent observed actions
abilities.description: Macaque recordings identified cells active during eating movements and while watching similar movements. Some also responded when another individual made a mouth gesture.

abilities.name: Recognize identity across images
abilities.description: In recordings from people viewing different images of one individual, some neurons responded across viewpoints and sometimes even to the written name.

abilities.name: Form words silently
abilities.description: In two people doing a limited word task, researchers could predict some silently spoken words from activity in a patch of parietal cortex.
abilities.evidence_quote: internally spoken and vocalized words were significantly decodable

nuances.claim: Human neuron counts break every primate scaling rule.
nuances.reality: About 86 billion neurons in the adult human brain fit the cellular scaling relationship examined for primates. This result concerns counts relative to brain size.
nuances.evidence_quote: expected for a primate of human proportions

nuances.claim: Modern humans always had larger brains than Neanderthals.
nuances.reality: Estimated skull-cavity volumes overlap. In one comparison, Neanderthals averaged 1,450 milliliters and present-day humans averaged 1,328 milliliters. Fossil skulls preserve a volume estimate, not a neuron count.
nuances.evidence_quote: present-day humans (mean, 1328 ml; SD, 164 ml) and Neandertals (mean, 1450 ml; SD, 189 ml)

connectome.description: H01 maps about one cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex. A separate comparative project traced color-related connections at the center of the retina in humans, macaques and marmosets.
connectome.evidence_quote: a cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex

additional_evidence.evidence_quote: We applied connectomic electron microscopy to the specialized foveal retina

connectome.project_scope: partial refers to local cortex or retina, depending on the project.

open_question.text: How do cells that recognize an individual across different pictures participate in forming a lasting memory?

passages.evidence_quote: endocranial volume estimates of our fossil reconstructions
